analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage to patients joining approved clinical trials.
analysis.headline: One sponsor, zero cosponsors, no committee action, no vote: the bill died in a House subcommittee before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred health plans from denying, limiting, or conditioning coverage of care a patient receives because the patient is enrolled in an approved clinical study, including care for problems caused by the study itself [S2]. It would not have required plans to pay for the research costs of the trial — only for the routine care that the plan would already cover if it were given outside a study [S3]. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with serious illnesses — most concretely cancer and other patients whose best remaining option is a clinical trial — would have kept their normal insurance coverage for routine care and for complications from the study, instead of facing coverage denial or reduced coverage because they enrolled [S2]. Medical researchers and trial sponsors would also have benefited, since fear of losing coverage is a known barrier that keeps patients from enrolling in studies [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Health plans could no longer deny, limit, or impose extra conditions on coverage of routine care simply because the patient is in an approved clinical study, and could not discriminate against enrollees for participating.
Coverage would extend to care for conditions resulting from participating in the study, protecting patients who suffer complications from a trial.
By removing the coverage penalty for enrolling, the bill would have made it easier for patients to join trials, which is how new treatments get tested and approved.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and health plans, which would have had to pay for routine items and services furnished inside approved studies that they could otherwise exclude or limit. The bill deliberately excluded trial research costs, so plans would not pay for the study itself, only for care they already cover outside trials [S3]. Some of that added cost would flow into premiums paid by all enrollees.

drawbacks.text: Health plans would have faced new mandated costs: they could no longer exclude routine care delivered inside a trial, an expense that would ultimately be spread across premiums.

The definition of an approved study is broad — it includes studies approved by qualified nongovernmental research entities, not just federal agencies — which would have widened the range of studies a plan must accommodate and invited disputes over what qualifies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection for patients is real and the cost to insurers is deliberately narrowed: plans never had to fund the research itself, only the routine care they would cover anyway outside a trial, plus care for trial complications. A good-faith objection is that plans would still absorb added claims and that the loose definition of an approved study could be stretched. On balance the trade favors patients, but the bill's narrow scope and lack of support suggest insurers and employers saw any mandate as opening the door to broader coverage requirements.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it sat until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Nita Lowey introduced the bill on June 5, 1996.
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day.
On June 21, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment — the last action of record.
The bill attracted no cosponsors and received no further action before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and health plans, which avoided a new mandate to cover routine care for trial participants. Patients in clinical trials gained nothing; the coverage gap the bill addressed stayed open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers avoided a coverage mandate

for.name: Nita Lowey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; after referral to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment on June 21, 1996, no hearing or markup is recorded.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman in the 104th Congress, controlled whether the bill ever reached the House floor; the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan split — only a Democratic sponsor and no visible support in either party.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped their ability to deny, limit, or condition coverage for patients in approved clinical trials, forcing them to pay for routine care they could otherwise exclude. Their interest lay in keeping that discretion, which is why the bill's death left the coverage gap in place.

industries.industry: Medical research and clinical trial sponsors (NIH, drug and device makers)
industries.note: Easier enrollment is the lifeblood of clinical research, and coverage denial is a known deterrent for patients deciding whether to join a trial. The bill would have made recruiting patients cheaper and faster for trial sponsors without costing them anything directly.
